key_insight: Amplitude damping mainly changes variational quantum circuit features by a zero-temperature bias, while its infinite-temperature twirl preserves contraction but removes that bias, so accuracy differences are often a feature-scaling effect rather than pure noise strength.
engineering_relevance: A trainable output scale can recover much of the lost accuracy, but the price shifts to higher measurement-shot cost, making noise-model choice and calibration important for practical quantum ML hardware deployment.
method: Compare amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled infinite-temperature counterpart in variational circuits
Analyze feature scaling, sampling cost, and depth dependence under random parameters and trained models
Study when damping direction is gauge-dependent versus physically meaningful in circuit layouts
evidence_signal: Across simulations up to eight qubits, AD and its twirls differ by only about 3 percentage points after output scaling, while a four-qubit classifier at p=0.3 and 10^3 shots/image stays within 1.5 points of noiseless accuracy under AD but loses up to 33 points under the twirled models.
watch_item: The damping direction can be a gauge only in certain circuit architectures; in decomposed two-qubit gates or eigensolver settings, it becomes a physical effect and cannot be ignored.
paper_title: Zero- Versus Infinite-Temperature Damping in Variational Quantum Circuits: Feature Scale, Sampling Cost, and Frame Gauge
